title: Project 1: command-line calculator
learningObjectives: Translate a calculator's requirements into a clear input grammar, supported operators, output format and error policy.
Separate parsing, arithmetic calculation and user interaction into small functions with explicit interfaces.
Use fgets and strtod safely to parse a complete expression, checking conversion progress, range errors, non-finite values and trailing characters.
Implement addition, subtraction, multiplication and division while validating operators, zero divisors and non-finite arithmetic results.
Design a command loop with a quit command, clear diagnostics, bounded input handling and recovery after invalid input.
Compile and test the calculator with strict C11 warnings, representative expressions, boundary values, malformed input and failure cases.

understand.concept: A command-line calculator reads an expression, validates its syntax, performs one arithmetic operation and displays a result. This project supports the grammar: number operator number, where number is a finite decimal value accepted by strtod and operator is +, -, * or /. A reliable program separates three responsibilities: parsing text into typed values, calculating from validated values, and interacting with the user. It rejects malformed expressions, unsupported operators, division by positive or negative zero, numeric conversion range errors and non-finite results.
understand.whyItMatters: This project combines functions, selection, numeric types, standard input, strings, error handling and testing into one small application. It also demonstrates why input must be treated as untrusted text: a successful-looking line may contain missing operands, extra characters, an unsupported operator or a value outside the representable range.
understand.analogy: Think of a calculator as a small service counter. The input desk checks that the request is complete and understandable; the calculation unit performs only supported operations; the display desk reports either a result or a clear reason the request could not be completed.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not define floating-point behaviour. C double values use finite precision, decimal fractions may not be represented exactly, and arithmetic can overflow to infinity or produce other exceptional values. This project deliberately rejects non-finite operands and results.

keyTerms.definition: Converting text into structured values while checking that the input follows a defined grammar.
A standard C library function that converts the initial part of a string to double and reports where conversion stopped.
A library error indicator that can report range errors such as ERANGE after numeric conversion.
A floating-point value that is neither infinity nor NaN; isfinite can test this property.
A fixed-size character array used to receive a line safely with fgets.
Keeping parsing, calculation and user interaction in separate functions so each can be tested independently.
A documented decision about which inputs or results are rejected and how the program reports them.

designRequirements.detail: One expression per line: finite number, one of + - * /, then finite number; optional surrounding whitespace; no trailing non-whitespace characters.
Reject missing operands, invalid numbers, unsupported operators, conversion range errors, trailing text and division by zero.
Reject non-finite results, including overflow to infinity; print finite results with a readable precision.
Accept multiple expressions until the user enters q or EOF; report an invalid line and continue.
Use fgets with a fixed buffer, detect overlong lines and drain the remainder before reading the next expression.

understand.history: Mechanical calculating devices predate electronic computers by centuries. Early electronic calculators introduced arithmetic circuits, while command-line calculators became common teaching projects because they expose the complete path from text input to validated computation. C's strtod function is part of the standard library and provides more control over numeric parsing than a simple unchecked input conversion.

explain.narrative:
Design the program before coding. The input grammar is one expression per line: a number, an operator (+, -, * or /), and another number. Whitespace may appear between fields, but no extra non-whitespace text is allowed. The interactive program repeats until q or end-of-file. Invalid input should produce a diagnostic and return to the prompt rather than terminating the whole session.

Use fgets to read a bounded line. Unlike an unbounded input operation, fgets limits how many characters are written into the destination buffer. If the buffer fills without a newline and the stream has not reached EOF, the line may be longer than the buffer; drain the rest of that line and reject it so its tail is not mistaken for a new expression.

Use strtod to parse each number. Set errno to zero before conversion, check that the end pointer moved, reject ERANGE and reject non-finite values with isfinite. Skip whitespace explicitly, read exactly one supported operator, parse the second number and then require the rest of the line to contain only whitespace. This prevents inputs such as 12abc + 3 or 1 + 2 extra from being silently accepted.

Keep arithmetic in a separate function. It should reject non-finite operands, unsupported operators and a divisor equal to 0.0 (which also catches negative zero). After the operation, check that the result is finite. Floating-point arithmetic is approximate: this project displays a finite result but does not promise exact decimal arithmetic for currency or accounting. A production money application should use an explicitly designed fixed-point or decimal representation and a documented rounding policy.

Example 1 tests the calculation function directly. It covers all four operations, division by zero, an unsupported operator and a result that overflows to a non-finite value. Example 2 is a complete interactive command-line calculator with safe line input, strict parsing, clear errors and a quit command. The examples use only standard C library facilities and do not require the HTML/CSS/JavaScript playground.

examples.title: Build and test the calculator arithmetic engine
examples.explanation: calculate accepts two finite double operands, a supported operator and a valid output pointer. It rejects division by zero before dividing and checks the computed value with isfinite before storing it. check_result tests normal arithmetic independently of user input. The remaining checks verify that division by zero, an unsupported operator, overflow to a non-finite result and a null output pointer are rejected. Exact equality is suitable for these selected integer-valued results; general floating-point calculations often need a tolerance-based comparison. The program intentionally tests the calculation layer separately from parsing and terminal interaction.

examples.title: Create a complete interactive command-line calculator
examples.explanation: skip_spaces uses isspace after converting each character to unsigned char, as required by the character-classification functions. parse_number uses strtod and checks that conversion consumed characters, errno is not ERANGE and the result is finite. parse_expression accepts exactly two numbers and one supported operator, then rejects trailing non-whitespace text. read_line uses fgets with a fixed-size buffer; if the line is too long, it drains the remainder so the next prompt starts with a fresh line. The main loop accepts repeated expressions and q, recovers from invalid input and reports arithmetic failures. The result is checked for finiteness before display. EOF exits cleanly. The project uses double for general arithmetic, not exact currency calculations.

practise.guidedTask: Trace these expressions through parsing and calculation: `8 * 3`, `15 / 4`, `9 / 0`, `12abc + 3`, `1 + 2 extra` and `q`. For each one, state whether parsing succeeds, whether calculation runs and what the user should see. Then add a test for negative zero as the divisor.
practise.independentTask: Extend the interactive calculator with a remainder operation for integer-only operands or add a power operation with a clearly documented numeric policy. Keep parsing, calculation and interaction separate. Add tests for leading/trailing whitespace, missing operands, multiple operators, unsupported operators, overlong input, EOF, conversion range errors, division by zero, non-finite results and repeated invalid lines. Document why binary floating-point is not appropriate for exact financial amounts.
hints: Define the expression grammar before parsing; decide whether signs belong to numbers and whether whitespace is permitted.
Check strtod's end pointer and errno after every conversion; a returned numeric value alone does not prove the whole token was valid.
Use fgets with a fixed buffer and detect an input line that does not fit; discard its remainder before reading again.
Separate parse_expression from calculate so each function can be tested without terminal input.
Compare a divisor with 0.0 to reject both positive and negative floating-point zero; check isfinite after arithmetic.
A double calculator is suitable for general demonstration arithmetic, but money needs a defined decimal/fixed-point representation and rounding policy.

questions.prompt: Why should parsing be separate from the arithmetic calculation function?
options: It allows text validation and arithmetic rules to be tested independently
It makes invalid input automatically valid
It removes the need to check division by zero
It guarantees exact decimal arithmetic
questions.answer: It allows text validation and arithmetic rules to be tested independently
questions.explanation: Separate functions have clearer responsibilities and can be tested with focused inputs.

questions.prompt: What should a robust strtod-based parser check?
options: That conversion advanced the end pointer, errno is not ERANGE and the value is finite
Only whether the returned value is nonzero
Only whether the input line contains a decimal point
Whether the operator appears before the first number
questions.answer: That conversion advanced the end pointer, errno is not ERANGE and the value is finite
questions.explanation: These checks reject missing conversions, range errors and non-finite values.

questions.prompt: Why does the calculator reject a divisor equal to 0.0?
options: To prevent a division-by-zero calculation, including a negative-zero divisor
Because C does not support the division operator
Because every decimal value is stored as zero
To force the result to be an integer
questions.answer: To prevent a division-by-zero calculation, including a negative-zero divisor
questions.explanation: The equality check with 0.0 matches both positive and negative floating-point zero.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of detecting an overlong input line after fgets?
options: To reject the incomplete line and discard its remaining characters
To execute the first part of the expression twice
To increase the buffer automatically without a limit
To skip numeric validation
questions.answer: To reject the incomplete line and discard its remaining characters
questions.explanation: Draining the rest prevents leftover characters from being treated as a separate next expression.

questions.prompt: Which statement about using double for a financial calculator is most accurate?
options: Binary floating-point may not represent decimal amounts exactly, so money needs a defined fixed-point or decimal policy
double always stores every decimal amount exactly
A double value prevents rounding errors in all operations
The printf format controls the internal precision of arithmetic
questions.answer: Binary floating-point may not represent decimal amounts exactly, so money needs a defined fixed-point or decimal policy
questions.explanation: Formatting changes how a value is displayed, not how it is represented or rounded internally.
